extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (aesthetics), readers of Kant
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual conditions for making and assessing judgements of taste (what counts as beautiful, pleasant, or good), as developed in a philosophical/aesthetic treatise. Focuses on disinterestedness, universality, purposiveness, and the cognitive faculties involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between sensation and feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensation (objective representation of sense) vs feeling (merely subjective, constituting no representation of an object). E.g., the green colour of meadows is objective sensation; the pleasantness of this is subjective sensation or feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to separate perceptual/copied qualities of objects from the subjective pleasures that do not represent objects; avoid conflating sensory representation with merely subjective affect when analyzing aesthetic responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasantness (taste of Sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasant gratifies and excites desire; it rests entirely upon sensation and is pathologically conditioned (by impulses, stimuli). It is immediate and tied to inclination (e.g., a spiced dish is 'pleasant' though not necessarily 'good').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat pleasant judgements as private, sensory reactions limited to the subject ('It is pleasant to me'). They do not by themselves claim universal validity and can be empirically studied and compared, not elevated to aesthetic universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good (mediated by concept and reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: What pleases through the mere concept (GOOD) involves a concept of purpose and the relation of reason to volition. Distinguishes 'good for something' (useful) from 'good in itself' (absolute/moral good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To call something 'good' requires a concept of what the object ought to be; the judgement of the Good is cognitive/practical and tied to reasons and purposes, not mere immediate sensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste defined as disinterested judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste is the faculty of judging an object or its representation by an entirely disinterested satisfaction or dissatisfaction; the object of such satisfaction is called beautiful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper aesthetic judgement must be free from personal inclinations, desires, and practical interests — evaluate beauty by the form of satisfaction, not by any advantage or personal gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty pleases universally without a concept
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful is that which, apart from concepts, is represented as the object of a universal satisfaction — the judgement of taste claims validity for everyone although it is not based on concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a 'beautiful' judgement, check (a) that it is not grounded in conceptual/cognitive reasons, and (b) that it purports a universal communicability of the pleasure (the speaker demands assent, not merely reports a private liking).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality of aesthetical judgement is subjective, not logical
rubrics_metrics.description: The universality claimed in judgements of taste is aesthetic (subjective) because it does not rest on concepts of the object; it imputes a general communicability of pleasure rather than objective logical validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish claims of subjective universal agreement (aesthetic universality) from logically grounded, concept-based universality (as in moral or cognitive judgements); do not treat aesthetic universality as proof of objective properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement of taste demands the 'universal voice'
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling something 'beautiful' is pronounced as if beauty were a property of the object; the judge speaks and demands agreement from others ('the thing is beautiful') rather than saying 'it is beautiful to me'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the speaker is making a mere personal report or asserting a claim to communal assent; aesthetic critique must account for this normative demand when responding to a judgement of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure in judgement of taste follows the judgement and is grounded in communicability
rubrics_metrics.description: In a judgement of taste the subjective capability of universal communication (of the mental state) is fundamental, and the pleasure in the object is consequent — the pleasure follows from the representation's universal communicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing aesthetic response, consider whether pleasure arises from a preceding sensation or from a judged harmony of faculties that one believes can be communicated to others; the latter indicates an aesthetic (not merely sensory) pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free play of Imagination and Understanding as the subjective condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of 'free play' between Imagination (gathering manifold of intuition) and Understanding (unity of concept) in a representation is the subjective condition whose universal communicability grounds judgements of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the representation elicits a harmonious, purposive-like interaction of cognitive faculties (without settling into a determinate concept); such harmonious free play is the psychological correlate of aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of purposiveness without purpose grounds beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is based on the form of the purposiveness of an object's representation (subjective purposiveness) without any objective or subjective purpose — 'purposiveness without purpose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate beauty in terms of formal purposiveness (how the form appears suited to cognitive faculties) rather than any practical or conceptual end; avoid importing teleological or utilitarian reasons into aesthetic appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement of taste excludes charm and emotion (disinterestedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every interest (charms, emotions) spoils the judgement of taste and takes from its impartiality; a pure judgement of taste has as its determining ground merely the purposiveness of the form and is independent of charm and emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming a pure aesthetic judgement, ensure that empirical pleasures (charm, sentimentality, personal emotion) are not being used as the basis of the judgement; such contamination makes the judgement empirical, not pure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between empirical and pure aesthetical judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical (material) aesthetical judgements assert pleasantness or unpleasantness (judgements of Sense); pure (formal) aesthetical judgements assert beauty of an object or manner of representation (judgements of Taste).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify aesthetic claims: if based on sensation/colour/tone => empirical/material; if based on form and disinterested purposiveness => pure/formal. This affects whether a judgement can claim universal validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant, Beautiful, and Good are distinct kinds of satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasant (that which gratifies), Beautiful (that which pleases), and Good (that which is esteemed/approved) designate different relations of representations to pleasure/pain: pleasant concerns animals, beautiful concerns human (animal+rational) beings, good concerns all rational beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating these categories: an object may be pleasant without being beautiful or good; in critique, identify which relation is operative before applying standards of purity, universality, or reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic universality arises from belief in shared conditions of judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the disinterested satisfaction feels free from private conditions, the judge attributes its ground to what he can presuppose in every other person and thus believes he has reason to expect similar satisfaction in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a judgement claims universality, interrogate the assumed shared cognitive conditions (capacity for free play of faculties) rather than objective properties of the object; universality is an imputative claim about others' faculties.
